title: The Use of Dietary Supplements

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For decades scientists have searched for evidence that vitamin C will protect us from colds and flu, and have mostly come up empty-handed – there’s more evidence that regular hand-washing will stop us catching a cold. So why, according to one recent survey in a western country, do more than 30% of people still take vitamin C or other supplements? Here’s one useful guideline: beware the phrase ‘scientific studies show’ when used about a product that is for sale. Scientific studies are complicated, mean little in isolation, and generally only make sense to people used to reading them – and even they can’t always agree.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: ‘One of the things that people seem to hate about science is that one week we’re saying one thing, and the next week another expert says something that completely contradicts that,’ says Mark Bolland, a senior researcher at the University of Auckland. The truth is that not all scientific studies are created equal. The most revealing type of study would be a randomised trial, when researchers take a group of people, divide them in half and give one group a supplement and the other a placebo. Drug companies are legally obliged to conduct such trials for new medicines. But companies selling supplements have no such obligations, and generally point to observational studies. However, observational trials just follow a group of people who are taking supplements anyway – usually educated females inclined to look after their health. Their better health, then, may have less to do with supplements and more to do with the people taking them, thus accounting for some of the apparent contradictions.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Here is something scientists do know: excessive quantities of life-giving consumables – water, oxygen, vitamins – can be dangerous. Recently, the Journal of the American Medical Association published the results of a randomised trial looking at whether supplements could protect against serious disease. The trial, involving 35,000 men, was eventually stopped after it seemed that taking the supplement had no benefits, and might even increase the risk of disease. One of the largest studies was conducted by the Cochrane Collaboration, which looked at 67 randomised trials on supplements. It found none of the supplements improved health, but vitamins A, E and beta-carotene were associated with an increased risk. ‘As far as I’m aware,’ says Rod Jackson, professor of epidemiology at the University of Auckland, ‘none of the recent randomised controlled trials has shown any benefits of vitamins. Folic acid before and during pregnancy appears to be one of the few exceptions.’

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The research into calcium supplements reflects much of the wider debate. An influential study published in the 1990s showed that calcium supplements reduced the risk of hip fractures by 40%. However, the sample for the study was women of a single nationality whose bones and lifestyle were unrepresentative of the wider population, which was the cause of some criticism. Studies that followed weren’t quite as persuasive, though they did show that calcium supplements improved bone density, which researchers believed might reduce the number of fractures. This, however, was an assumption, so Ian Reid, professor of medicine and endocrinology at the University of Auckland, decided to find out if it was actually true. Using a large, randomised study, Reid’s results were confounding: calcium made little difference to bones, was beneficial to cholesterol and blood-pressure levels, but also seemed to be associated with an increased risk of heart failure.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: To ensure these results were reliable, one of Reid’s team members, researcher Mark Bolland, began gathering all the data from existing trials and confirmed Reid’s discovery. Neither of these studies was well received in some other quarters, including by some scientists. But, says Bolland, ‘…two years later, no-one has yet disproved it.’ What people want to know, though, is whether women should take calcium supplements. Bolland replies that it depends on your definitions: to his mind, safety is about weighing things up carefully. In the case of calcium supplements, there are possible serious side effects, so they cannot be recommended. Evidently, local general practitioners have taken the results on board; in the last six years, says Bolland, prescriptions of calcium have dropped by 60 per cent.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Calcium isn’t the whole story, though. Currently the most fashionable supplement isn’t a vitamin or mineral, but a long-chain fatty acid, known as omega-3. We can’t manufacture it synthetically but we can get it from our diet, mainly from oily fish like tuna or from fish-oil capsules. Victoria University professor Shaun Holt recommends omega-3, in fish or supplementary form. ‘There’s evidence that omega-3s are good for over 30 health conditions, and the evidence that they are good for your heart is rock solid,’ says Holt. Welma Stonehouse, associate professor of human nutrition at Massey University, agrees. She’s sceptical about most dietary supplements, but takes omega-3 regularly. Murray Skeaff, professor of human nutrition at the University of Otago, is also not convinced about the value of taking supplements. He says, ‘There is a massive accumulation of evidence to show if you want to prevent disease and prolong life, the best way to do it is having a good diet. The evidence for supplements just pales in comparison.’

subtitle:
Many people take supplementary vitamins and minerals – usually tablets taken daily in additionto a regular diet. The scientific evidence to support this practice
is now being questioned
